name: MTU, Fragmentation and Path MTU
intent: How the largest packet a link carries shapes TCP segment size, why fragmentation hurts, and why filtering ICMP creates connections that work for small requests and hang on large ones.
scenario: A client downloads 100,000 bytes over a path of three links. Two have an MTU of 1,500 bytes; the middle one is a tunnel with 100 bytes of overhead, so it carries only 1,400. The same transfer is run with ICMP allowed, ICMP blocked, the DF bit cleared and with MSS clamping.
problem: A link has a Maximum Transmission Unit, the largest IP packet it carries. Ethernet is typically 1,500 bytes, and every tunnel, VPN or overlay makes the usable size smaller. A sender does not know the smallest MTU on the path, and a router that cannot forward a packet has to either split it or drop it. When the message that explains the drop is filtered, the sender never learns and the connection hangs: handshakes and small requests work, so monitoring looks fine, and only large responses stall.

howItWorks.title: MTU and MSS: packet size versus segment size
howItWorks.text: The MTU is the largest IP packet a link can carry, headers included. TCP's Maximum Segment Size (MSS) is the data bytes per segment. With 20 bytes of IP header and 20 bytes of TCP header, MSS = MTU - 40: 1,460 for a 1,500 byte MTU. Each side announces its MSS in the SYN, based on its own interface, which says nothing about links further along the path.

howItWorks.title: A packet bigger than the link: fragment or drop
howItWorks.text: If the Don't Fragment (DF) bit is clear, the router splits the packet into fragments that fit. Fragment data is a multiple of 8 bytes, so a 1,500 byte packet on a 1,400 byte link becomes 2 fragments of at most 1,376 data bytes. Only the destination reassembles them. If DF is set, which is typical for TCP, the router drops the packet instead and (typically) sends an ICMP 'fragmentation needed' message with the next-hop MTU.

howItWorks.title: Fragmentation is costly, not just slow
howItWorks.text: Each fragment repeats an IP header, middleboxes and firewalls often drop fragments or must reassemble them to inspect them, and the loss of any one fragment loses the whole packet, so retransmission resends all of it. In the sample, 1% fragment loss means 9,900 of 10,000 whole packets arrive, but 9,801 when each packet needs 2 fragments, and the transfer sends 138 fragments for 69 packets.

howItWorks.title: Path MTU Discovery learns the limit from the drop
howItWorks.text: With DF set, the sender relies on ICMP to learn the smallest MTU on the path (Path MTU Discovery). It sends a full-size segment, a router drops it and replies with the limit, and the sender lowers its segment size and retransmits. In the sample, which sends one full-size packet first, it costs one wasted packet and one round trip: 75 packets sent in total, with an MSS of 1,360 instead of 1,460. A real sender may have a whole window of full-size segments in flight, and all of them are dropped and resent. The mechanism is RFC 1191 for IPv4 and RFC 8201 for IPv6. This is why ICMP 'fragmentation needed' must be allowed through firewalls.

howItWorks.title: Blocking ICMP creates a black hole
howItWorks.text: If ICMP is filtered the sender never hears about the drop. The handshake and small requests use small packets that fit, so the connection opens and looks healthy. The first full-size data segment is dropped, silently and every time it is retried: the transfer stalls with 0 bytes delivered. A 1,000 byte response still works. The symptom is 'small pages load, big downloads and uploads hang', typically only through a VPN or from certain networks. Some stacks work around it by probing for a working size (packetization-layer PMTUD, RFC 4821; off by default for TCP on Linux), but you should not rely on it.

howItWorks.title: MSS clamping avoids needing PMTUD
howItWorks.text: A tunnel endpoint or firewall can rewrite the MSS in passing SYN packets to the tunnel's limit minus 40: 1,360 here. Both ends then send segments that fit, with no wasted packet and no dependence on ICMP: 74 packets, 0 extra round trips, even with ICMP blocked. Clamping only fixes TCP and only if it is applied on the path the SYN takes; UDP, QUIC and other protocols must size their own datagrams (QUIC typically starts conservatively, near 1,200 bytes).

pros: A larger MTU means fewer packets and less header overhead for bulk transfers
Path MTU Discovery lets senders adapt to any path without configuration
MSS clamping fixes tunnel problems in one place, with no change to clients or servers
Cleared DF plus fragmentation at least keeps traffic flowing when ICMP is broken
cons: Every tunnel, VPN, overlay or encapsulation subtracts from the MTU, and the sender cannot see it
Fragmentation multiplies per-packet loss, wastes header bytes and is often filtered
PMTUD depends on ICMP messages that many firewalls drop
MTU black holes are partial failures: monitoring based on small requests stays green
whenToUse: Planning tunnels, VPNs and overlay networks: subtract the encapsulation overhead and set interface MTUs and MSS clamps deliberately
Diagnosing 'works for small requests, hangs for large ones' with ping at fixed sizes and the DF bit set
Allowing ICMP type 3 code 4 (and ICMPv6 type 2, 'packet too big') through every firewall on the path
Choosing a conservative datagram size for UDP-based protocols and probing upward
whenNotToUse: Raising MTU to jumbo frames (typically 9,000) across a path you do not control: every hop must support it
Relying on fragmentation as the normal way to cross a small-MTU link
Blocking all ICMP as a security measure: it breaks PMTUD while stopping little
Clamping MSS lower than needed 'to be safe' on links that do not need it: it costs throughput for nothing
pitfalls: Blocking ICMP 'fragmentation needed': handshakes succeed, large transfers stall, and nobody can say why
Testing with small requests only: a health check of 300 bytes never exercises the path MTU
Forgetting that every tunnel layer shrinks the MTU: IPsec inside a VPN inside an overlay can lose a hundred bytes or more
Assuming IPv6 can fragment in routers: it cannot, only the sender fragments, so a sender must either run PMTUD or keep packets at the 1,280 byte IPv6 minimum MTU
Clearing DF to 'fix' a black hole: it works but every large packet doubles into fragments, and fragment loss is amplified
Setting MSS clamp on one direction or one path only: asymmetric paths can still send oversized segments
Confusing MTU with MSS: a 1,500 byte MTU gives 1,460 bytes of TCP data, not 1,500

roles.label: Sender
roles.description: Chooses the segment size from its MSS and reacts to ICMP messages.

roles.label: Router
roles.description: Forwards, fragments or drops a packet that exceeds the next link's MTU.

roles.label: Tunnel endpoint
roles.description: Adds encapsulation overhead and can clamp the MSS in SYN packets.

roles.label: Firewall
roles.description: May filter ICMP and fragments, which decides whether PMTUD works.

quiz.question: Through a VPN, small web pages load but large downloads hang forever. Pings with small packets succeed. Which cause fits best?
options: The server's TCP window is too small
A packet larger than the tunnel's MTU is dropped and the ICMP message about it is filtered
The DNS server returns the wrong address for large files
TLS session tickets expire during large downloads
quiz.explanation: Handshakes and small requests fit within the MTU, so the connection opens. Full-size segments are dropped, and without the ICMP 'fragmentation needed' message the sender never shrinks them. That produces exactly this pattern.

quiz.question: A 1,500 byte packet with the DF bit set meets a link with an MTU of 1,400. What does a standard router do?
options: Splits it into two fragments and forwards both
Drops it and, typically, sends an ICMP message with the link's MTU
Queues it until a larger link becomes available
quiz.explanation: DF forbids fragmentation, so the router drops the packet and normally reports the next-hop MTU back to the sender. If DF were clear it would fragment instead.

quiz.question: A tunnel carries 1,400 byte packets and ICMP is blocked on the path. Which change makes TCP transfers work without depending on ICMP?
options: Setting the sender's initial congestion window to 100 segments
Clamping the MSS in SYN packets at the tunnel endpoint to 1,360
quiz.explanation: MSS clamping makes both ends choose segments that already fit the tunnel (1,400 minus 40 bytes of headers), so no oversized packet is ever sent. Window sizes and timestamps do not change packet size.
